tagline: Coastal curves connect a quarried rock, a creamery town and elephant seals.
intro: Highway 1 leaves San Luis Obispo on four lanes, rejoins the coast at Morro Bay and becomes a winding two-lane road beyond Cayucos, with occasional passing lanes. The Federal Highway Administration lists this North Coast corridor as a 57-mile All-American Road, highlighting Hearst Castle, Morro Estuary, the Pacific and opportunities for hiking, biking and kayaking. Its archived guide allows one hour to drive the byway or two hours to see it.

The coast road took shape in pieces. In 1921, legislation extended Route 56 south along the county road to Cambria; a further extension reached San Luis Obispo in 1931. The adjoining Carmel-San Simeon Highway opened in 1937 after 18 years of construction, linking existing county highways at its ends. Later changes carried traffic away from town streets: Highway 1 was rerouted to bypass Cayucos in 1965.

Traveling north from San Luis Obispo, reach Morro Bay and its harbor rock, then Cayucos and the former creamery community of Harmony. Cambria comes next, with one of the California mainland’s three native Monterey pine populations, followed by San Simeon and access to Hearst Castle. Continue past the elephant seal colony at Piedras Blancas toward San Carpóforo Creek, just south of the Monterey County line.

moments.title: Morro Rock
moments.text: Morro Rock, a volcanic plug, was once surrounded by water at the harbor entrance. Several kinds of birds nest on the rock, including three cormorant species and two gull species. Its stone helped reshape that harbor. Quarrying between 1889 and 1969 supplied the Morro Bay breakwater and improvements at Port San Luis Harbor. The Salinan and Chumash tribes consider the rock sacred. It is protected as Morro Rock State Preserve and serves as a peregrine falcon reserve. The Army built the road and breakwater that connected the rock to the mainland.
moments.notice: The causeway links the volcanic rock to the mainland at the harbor entrance.

moments.title: Harmony
moments.text: Harmony fits on one block, with a former creamery wrapping a small plaza in a U-shaped building. Swiss and Italian immigrants founded the creamery in 1869 after fires and drought made crop farming difficult in the coastal hills. The Harmony Valley Dairy Co-op began in 1901; the community also supported a stable, a blacksmith and a one-room school. The surviving dairy building dates to 1908. The creamery closed in 1955; in the 1970s, craftworkers took over its buildings. Its one-block layout even shaped a parade: participants in the former Doo Dah parade stayed put while spectators walked past them.
moments.notice: The former creamery forms a U around a small plaza.

moments.title: Piedras Blancas
moments.text: The Piedras Blancas lighthouse has lost its top, but it continues to serve navigation. Its first-order Fresnel lens was first lit on February 15, 1875. Earthquakes damaged the tower, and a final shock in 1948 led to removal of the upper three floors. The light was automated in 1975, when the sound signal was removed and the station became unmanned. The lens moved to Cambria, where it is on display. About a mile south of the lighthouse, elephant seals began using a rookery in 1990. The rookery has a boardwalk for viewing the animals, a separate coastal feature from the light station itself.
moments.notice: The lighthouse is missing its ornate upper floors.
